title: AppLovin: Deep Dive Analysis
content_html:
What Does the Company Do?

AppLovin is best understood as an advertising tech company, now powered by AI. Its job is to help businesses find customers who are likely to spend money, while helping app publishers earn as much as possible from the advertising space they sell.

Simply put, the only thing more annoying about this company than its name is what it actually does. Have you ever played a game on your phone and been interrupted by an annoying ad? Bingo! There’s a decent chance AppLovin was somewhere in the chain - either serving the ad or mediating the auction that put it there.

The centre of the business is AppLovin Ads, powered by AppLovin’s proprietary Axon AI engine. Until recently, the core user-acquisition product was called Axon Ads Manager. An advertiser tells AppLovin what result it wants, such as a target return on advertising spend. Axon then analyses enormous amounts of data and automatically decides which users should see which ads, where, and at what price. Advertisers generally keep spending as long as AppLovin delivers sufficiently profitable customers.

On the other side sits MAX, AppLovin’s monetisation platform. When an app has an advertising slot available, MAX runs a real-time auction between advertising networks to obtain the highest available price for that impression. In this way, AppLovin connects the two sides of the digital advertising market: businesses wanting customers and publishers wanting to monetise their audiences.

The company also owns Adjust, which measures advertising performance and attribution, and Wurl, which extends AppLovin into connected-TV advertising and distribution.

For the purpose of understanding the business, it’s important to note that AppLovin is no longer primarily a mobile-gaming company. It sold its Apps business in June 2025 and today operates essentially as a pure advertising technology business.

In practical terms, AppLovin sells a proposition of better advertising economics. Advertisers pay it to acquire profitable customers and publishers use it to maximise the value of their advertising inventory.

So, why has it been AppHatin lately?

Why Is It Hated?

AppLovin is hated because the market has moved from pricing extraordinary execution as permanent to questioning whether it can be not only sustained but repeated at all.

After revenue growth of 70% in2025, AppLovin reached its record closing high of $733.60 on Dec 22, 2026. By the end of the year, it traded around 50x forward earnings. Have we mentioned priced for perfection? There was massive confidence in Axon, continued gaming share gains and a successful expansion into consumer advertising baked into the valuation.

That confidence began to shake as soon as 2026 hit the calendar. Shares fell 30% in January alone as (expensive) software stocks got de-rated in broad SaaSpocalypse. Particularly for AppLovin, the perfect storm included a short-seller report that revived governance concerns and Google’s Project Genie released a genie in a form of fears of AI disruption. The latter arguably made very little fundamental sense after AppLovin sold its gaming studios, but it demonstrated really well how fragile sentiment had become, and how literally anything can be used as an excuse when the market wants to tank a stock badly enough.

Feb 2026 added another layer of AppLovin becoming AppHatin. The company beat Q4 revenue expectations and guided Q1 above consensus, yet shares still fell after earnings as investors focused on competition from Meta and broader AI disruption fears. Later in February, another hit came when the SEC confirmed that its investigation involving AppLovin remained ‘active and ongoing’. In March, industry checks raised separate concerns that AppLovin’s promising e-commerce product could struggle to scale efficiently as advertisers increased budgets.

All of this bearish development was not linear, though. Q1 was exceptional with revenue growing 59%, guidance beat, and the stock rallied 37% in May. Then, June brought another 16% decline amid the broader SaaSpocalypse, due to the most common reason of SaaS sell-off in 2026 - “Why Not”, followed by a 13% one-day drop in July when third-party data suggested slower e-commerce advertiser adoption.

As a result, AppLovin was already roughly 38% down YTD by the start of August. Then, while shareholders called for “stop, it’s already dead”, the Q2 print brought more carnage and it somewhat validated the market’s biggest fear. Revenue still grew 53%, but a small miss caused by slower Axon model improvements broke AppLovin’s near-unbroken pattern of beating elevated expectations. When the result is anything less than expected “exceptional”, combined with horrendous broad sentiment, the combination is lethal. The shares fell another 20%.

Ironically, AppLovin simultaneously disclosed that the SEC had concluded its inquiry with no recommended action, removing one of the largest overhangs. The market basically didn’t care. At all. So, what happens when every negative - no matter how small - is exaggerated to double-digit tanking of stock and even major positives are overlooked with small to none reaction?

That is the Hated Moats setup, alright! The fundamentals remain exceptional, but trust in their durability has collapsed.

Competitive Moat & Peer Comparison

The Moat

AppLovin’s moat is primarily a performance and data advantage, not traditional customer lock-in.

At the centre is Axon, the AI system that decides which advertisements to show, to whom and how much to bid for them. Every campaign and auction produces additional information about what converts, what customers are worth and what advertisers can profitably pay. At scale, that creates a flywheel where more advertising activity produces more data, better predictions improve advertiser returns, and better returns encourage advertisers to spend more. AppLovin explicitly describes this relationship in its filings.

MAX strengthens the other side of this system. It helps app publishers auction their advertising inventory across competing bidders in real time. This gives AppLovin substantial access to mobile advertising supply while Axon brings advertiser demand. This synergistic combination is understandably more important than either product alone.

There is good evidence that the entire system has genuinely improved. In 2025, AppLovin’s advertising revenue grew 70%, even though the number of installations increased only 3%. The much larger driver was a 72% increase in net revenue per installation, largely attributed to better Axon performance. And that’s important because growth wasn’t primarily coming from generating dramatically more installations. AppLovin was earning substantially more net revenue per installation, consistent with materially better Axon performance.

The financial results are consistent with this powerful business model. In 2025, AppLovin generated $5.48B of revenue, a 62.6% continuing-operations net margin and an 82.3% adjusted EBITDA margin. Reported FCF was nearly $4B, although that figure also includes cash flows from the discontinued Apps business prior to its June divestiture. We would be careful, however, about directly comparing these margins with every ad-tech peer because revenue recognition and business models differ across the industry. The economics are exceptional, but margins alone don’t prove the moat (especially a durable one).

Importantly, switching costs are weaker than they might appear at first. AppLovin itself says customers generally have no long-term commitments and can stop using its products at any time. Advertisers also commonly use several advertising platforms simultaneously. This means the moat depends on AppLovin continuing to deliver superior returns. Customers stay and increase budgets because Axon makes them money, not because they are trapped in a deeply embedded complex system.

Share Hated Moats

The Competition

The mentioned makes competition particularly important.

Within mobile gaming, Unity is the closest direct rival. But as AppLovin moves beyond gaming, the real competitive benchmark becomes Meta , Google and increasingly Amazon . All three possess enormous advertiser bases, huge datasets and world-class AI capabilities. AppLovin itself identifies Meta, Google, Amazon and Unity as major competitors. The Trade Desk and other programmatic platforms compete for some of the same advertising dollars, but they are less direct comparisons.

This leads to the most important question in the entire moat analysis, i.e. does AppLovin have a great gaming-advertising moat, or is the company at the beginnings of a much broader advertising moat?

There are encouraging signs. Consumer advertising spend in Q2 2026 was already roughly 28% above Q4 2025 levels, despite Q4 normally being the strongest seasonal period, suggesting that some non-gaming advertisers are seeing attractive returns. But gaming still represents the majority of revenue, and success against Meta and Google in e-commerce, financial services and other consumer categories is far from proven.

There’s also an unusual weakness embedded within the moat itself. Axon must keep getting better, which might not be as easy as it’s been historically and Q2 2026 demonstrated this clearly. When model improvements were smaller than usual, sequential growth slowed. Management openly acknowledged that there is no guarantee meaningful AI improvements will arrive neatly every quarter.

The conclusion of our analysis suggests that AppLovin already has a strong moat in mobile-gaming advertising, created by the combination of Axon, proprietary performance data, MAX distribution and enormous transaction scale. But it’s still a performance moat, not a lock-in moat.

Its future strength basically depends on two things - whether Axon can continue outperforming competing systems, and whether that advantage transfers beyond gaming. If both happen, AppLovin could become one of the few serious performance-advertising alternatives to Meta and Google. However, If they don’t come true, today’s exceptional moat may ultimately prove much narrower than the financial results suggest.

Recent Stock Performance & Market Sentiment

AppLovin’s share-price reset has become far more severe than the deterioration in its underlying business, that’s quite obvious. The stock closed August 19, 2026 at $310.94, leaving it down roughly 54% YTD. Around $145B of equity value has disappeared from its highs.

The latest earnings release accelerated the decline. AppLovin fell almost 20% in the session following Q2 results, despite reporting numbers that would look exceptional for almost any other company. Revenue increased 53% YoY to $1.92B, net income from continuing operations rose 64% to $1.27B, adjusted EBITDA climbed 58% to $1.61B, and FCF reached $863M.

The problem was, as we mentioned above, that the revenue came in slightly below consensus with Q3 guidance of $2.06B-$2.09B, while still implying approximately 46% to 48% growth, which was around or slightly below Wall Street forecasts. AppLovin had built a reputation for repeated beat-and-raise quarters. Simply delivering excellent growth was simply no longer enough.

Notably, the management attributed the softer result largely to fewer meaningful improvements to its Axon AI models during the quarter. A larger model upgrade arrived shortly afterwards, and management said advertiser demand and competitive positioning remained healthy. Nevertheless, this quarter exposed an important risk. AppLovin’s extraordinary growth increasingly depends on its algorithms continuing to improve advertising returns at an exceptional pace. Thus, the question has emerged - to what extent is that sustainable?

Our research suggests that Wall Street remains broadly positive about the company, but confidence has clearly fallen. Multiple analysts reduced price targets after Q2, reflecting lower expectations rather than a belief that the business is broken.

As a result, the debate is becoming unusually interesting. Bears see an ad-tech company whose growth depends on unpredictable AI improvements and whose previous valuation allowed virtually no room for disappointment combined with progressive deceleration while the bulls see a company still growing above 50%, generating extraordinary margins and cash flow, and beginning to penetrate advertising markets far larger than mobile gaming.

By all means, the sell-off of 2026 looks more like a collapse in expectations than a collapse in fundamentals.

In our view, AppLovin is becoming interesting precisely because the market has moved from assuming almost everything will go right to questioning whether its exceptional growth can continue at all.

Fundamental Analysis

Revenue Growth

One word? Exceptional. AppLovin’s core advertising business has exploded in recent years. Continuing revenue jumped from $1.84B in 2023 to $3.22B in 2024, and then to $5.48B in 2025. That’s +75% YoY growth in 2024 and +70% in 2025. That’s +75% YoY growth in 2024 and +70% in 2025 (continuing ops). By comparison, AppLovin’s Apps segment (games/publisher network) was flat-to-down (roughly $1.77B in 2022 to $1.44B in 2023 to $1.49B in 2024), so virtually all the top‐line expansion came from Advertising.

Advertising/Software Platform revenue compounded at roughly 69% annually from 2021 to 2024. The latest quarterly results confirm robust demand. In Q2 2026, revenue was $1.924B, +53% YoY. Management’s Q3 2026 guidance implies roughly 46–48% YoY growth, still exceptional but representing further deceleration from Q1’s 59% and Q2’s 53% growth.

Growth has been driven by greater advertiser uptake and higher spend on AppLovin’s AI-driven ad platform. AppLovin reports that “Axon Ads Manager comprises the vast majority of revenue”. The Advertising segment’s revenues (fees on publisher inventory) rose from $1.05B in 2022 to $3.2B in 2024, reflecting both new advertiser acquisition and increased ad budgets from existing clients. The apps/games business, in contrast, has been flat and is being wound down (sold in mid-2025). As a result, the consolidated business mix shifted dramatically. Advertising increased from roughly 37% of consolidated revenue in 2022 to 68% in 2024. Following the sale of Apps in June 2025, the remaining operating business is entirely advertising, and Apps is reported as discontinued operations.

Business & Segment Mix

AppLovin historically split its business into 2 segments, Advertising (ad-tech platform) and Apps (in-app purchases and ad revenue in its own gaming apps), but after selling the Apps business (closed June 2025), the company now reports only a single Advertising segment. In 2024, Advertising revenue was $3.224B and growing 75% YoY, whereas Apps revenue was $1.485B and roughly flat. Segment profitability reflects this shift where the Advertising segment produced $2.44B of “Adjusted EBITDA” in 2024 (i.e., 76% of its revenue) versus only $277m from Apps (i.e., 19% margin). On the old consolidated basis including Apps, Adjusted EBITDA margin rose from roughly 46% in 2023 to 58% in 2024. On today’s recast continuing-operations basis, excluding Apps, Adjusted EBITDA margin increased from 67.1% to 74.8%.

In short, growth is concentrated in the high-margin advertising platform, while the lower-margin apps business is phased out. We note that historically AppLovin’s growth was partly propped up by acquisitions (e.g. Wurl, MoPub) and volatile apps monetisation, but post-2024 essentially all growth is “organic” within advertising. No single advertiser is disclosed as dominant, and the large increase in Total Platform revenue suggests broad-based demand from many customers. During our research, we haven’t observed unusual customer concentration in the filings which would pose as a potential risk to the business.

Customer Metrics

AppLovin doesn’t report a single user count or ARR metric like a typical SaaS, and if you read some of our previous work, you know we’re a big fans of transparency in reporting the key metrics (hi, Netflix!). Although, the company does hint at platform usage trends.

Substantially all revenue comes from AppLovin Ads, where advertiser pricing is determined dynamically based on campaign goals and AppLovin reports revenue net of amounts paid to publishers. MAX separately generates revenue based on a percentage of client spend. In Q2 2026, management noted “strong consumer vertical momentum” and double-digit growth even among existing customers. Implicit KPIs include the number of active advertisers and the net revenue retention (NRR) from them. The sharp rebound in Adjusted EBITDA suggests that not only have new advertisers come on board but existing ones are also spending more, which is very important and positive fact in our view.

Unfortunately, AppLovin doesn’t disclose advertiser count, retention, NRR or ARPU, which limits our ability to separate growth from new customers versus expansion within existing accounts. Management said Q2 consumer advertiser spend finished 28% above Q4 2025 levels and indicated that much of the momentum reflected success among the existing customer base. Historically, AppLovin has also disclosed that net revenue per installation increased 72% in 2025 while installations rose only 3%, providing much stronger evidence of improved monetisation than any inferred ARPU or NRR metric.

Profitability & Margins

AppLovin’s profitability has improved dramatically as it scales. Gross profit on continuing (Advertising) operations was $4.816B in 2025 on $5.481B rev, i.e. 87.9% gross margin. This compares to 80.6% in 2023 and 83.9% in 2024. That is, by all means, impressive. The improvement reflects enormous operating leverage within the advertising business itself. Revenue grew 70% in 2025 while cost of revenue increased only 28%, driving continuing-operation gross margin from 83.9% to 87.9%.

Operating income has improved significantly as well, being $4.152B in 2025, up from $772m in 2023. That means an operating margin of 75.8% in 2025, versus 41.9% in 2023 and 59.3% in 2024. Again, at least on paper, that looks astonishing. Also, the corporate cost base has remained quite modest relative to sales with combined SG&A and R&D being only $663m in 2025 (i.e., 12% of revenue). Simply put, AppLovin’s software platform business is a highly scalable enterprise where each incremental $1 of revenue flows through at very high margins.

The operating leverage is even more striking in the expense base. Revenue grew 70% in 2025, while sales & marketing fell 19% to $204M and R&D fell 40% to $227M and G&A increased 42% to $234M. Combined S&M, R&D and G&A fell roughly 16% even as revenue increased by $2.26B. Management attributed much of the decline in S&M and R&D to lower personnel-related costs, including lower stock-based compensation, with S&M also benefiting from reduced headcount. The lower accounting R&D expense doesn’t necessarily imply under-investment. AppLovin still had roughly 42% of employees in R&D-related roles, but this is an area worth monitoring given how dependent future growth is on Axon improvements.

Comparisons to peers

AppLovin’s gross margins (88%) and operating margins (76%) are among the highest in ad tech. Traditional ad networks and DSPs often run 20-30% operating margins or less, given higher cost structures. AppLovin’s continuing-business Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 82.3% in 2025, while GAAP operating margin was an extraordinary 75.8%. That GAAP operating margin already includesSBC, which was roughly $208M from continuing operations in 2025. The profitability therefore remains exceptional even without relying solely on adjusted metrics. We are generally sceptical of any sole focus on “Adjusted EBITDA” (which excludes SBC and other items). Here, GAAP profit is solid on an absolute basis, not just a vanity metric.

Earnings Quality

AppLovin’s GAAP earnings growth is authentic rather than just “accounting trickery” in order to look impressive on earnings call. The main recurring non-cash costs are SBC and D&A/write-offs. Continuing-operations SBC fell from $357M in 2024 to $208M in 2025, while D&A/write-offs were about $131M. This is about 3.8% of 2025 revenue, a manageable level that is falling as a share of the business. There were still some one-off, when 2025 included a $189M goodwill impairment tied to the Apps sale and a $50M impairment of AppLovin’s investment in Humans.

The tax rate did fluctuate heavily. Continuing operations had only $22M of tax expense in 2024, before the effective rate rose to 13.1% in 2025.

Most EPS growth from 2023-2025 came from genuine operating leverage. Continuing revenue rose 198%, while continuing net income increased from $458M to $3.43B, with a modest additional benefit from lower share count.

In fact, AppLovin’s 2025 continuing net income of $3.43B on $5.48B revenue, a 62.6% net margin, suggests extraordinarily high earnings quality. Over half of each dollar of sales flows to the bottom line. That’s truly impressive since this is real cash profit, not an artifact of write-offs. One should note that diluted EPS rose from $0.98 in 2023 to $9.75 in 2025, largely reflecting this profit expansion, not just fewer shares. In oher words, AppLovin’s headline earnings and EPS have been driven by booming sales and excellent cost control, not by aggressive and “creative” accounting.

Free Cash Flow

AppLovin is a definition of cash machine. In 2025, operating cash flow was $3.971B and free cash flow, after capex and finance-lease principal payments, was $3.952B. Reported FCF/revenue rose from roughly 12% in 2021 to 72% in 2025, although 2025 FCF still includes cash flows from the discontinued Apps business.

The working capital changes are modest relative to income. For example, in 2025 accounts receivable rose $542M but this was easily covered by the profit inflows. Inventory is negligible (digital goods) and deferred revenues or prepaid are small.

FCF per share has likewise exploded. Using diluted shares outstanding, FCF per share in 2025 was roughly $11.5 (3,924/341.97M). That dwarfs the 2021 figure of $1.0 per share (345/342M). The FCF conversion (FCF/net income) is more than 100% now (about 118% in 2025) implying that earnings fully convert to cash. We note that 2022 FCF was held back by one-time MoPub publisher-migration incentives. Acquisition purchase prices themselves sit in investing cash flow and so they don’t reduce FCF.

Stock-Based Compensation & Dilution

SBC has been a large expense historically, but it’s declining as a fraction of the business. As noted above, SBC was $376M in 2024 and $210M in 2025. Relative to revenue this fell from 12% to 4%.

Share count has actually declined despite SBC. Weighted-average diluted shares fell from 362.6M in 2023 to 342.0M in 2025; actual shares outstanding at year-end 2025 were 338.3M. The reason behind this is, of course, the company’s buyback programs. The company spent $2.192B buying back shares in 2025 (retiring millions of shares). In effect, new shares from SBC were more than offset by repurchases. So EPS and FCF have risen faster per share than in absolute terms.

One caveat here, though. These repurchases were made at relatively high prices with an average price of roughly $400 per share. But on balance, shareholders today own slightly fewer shares than in prior years, so dilution risk is controlled (for now). The weighted-average diluted share count fell about 1.7% from 2024 to 2025, and roughly 5.7% from 2023 to 2025.

Balance Sheet

The balance sheet is very strong. As of end-2025, AppLovin had $2.49B in cash versus $3.51B of long-term debt, i.e. net debt of $1.02B. With 2025 EBITDA around $4.35B, net leverage is roughly 0.25x, i.e., negligible. As far as debt maturities go, the old 2018 credit facility was refinanced in December 2024 with $3.55B of unsecured notes carrying maturities from 2029 through 2054.

Interest expense fell sharply in 2025, primarily because the December 2024 refinancing replaced higher-cost floating-rate term loans with lower-cost fixed-rate notes. Working capital is ample with receivables being $1.819B on current liabilities of $1.334B, so liquidity is high (current ratio approximately 3.3x).

Contractual obligations are manageable, although AppLovin had $703M of non-cancelable purchase commitments, primarily for cloud computing, with $399M due within 12 months. Goodwill on the BS is $1.54B (mostly from acquisitions) against equity of $2.13B. Overall, we believe the balance sheet could easily support continued organic growth and even small tuck-in acquisitions. The company has no dividend, so cash can be deployed flexibly.

Capital Allocation

Over the past 5 years, AppLovin has invested modestly in R&D (bringing total for R&D and CapEx to $300-400M per year lately) and in acquisitions, and returned large sums via buybacks.

When we look at the key transactions, the company acquired the CTV ad platform Wurl in 2022, and spent approximately $1.03B in cash acquiring Twitter’s MoPub business in 2022. These have added some peripheral value (Wurl is still a small part of revenues). Most recent, AppLovin sold its Apps business for $400M + equity in 2025. The net proceeds went to pay down debt and fund buybacks (good capital allocation in this case, in our view).

Cumulatively through 2025, AppLovin spent roughly $4.7B on actual share repurchases under its buyback program. That has had the effect of shrinking the share count and boosting EPS. We note that virtually no buybacks are earmarked as “offset dilution” only. They are open-market or private purchases.

On the positive side, this disciplined repurchasing reflects management’s decision to use excess cash to benefit shareholders. Return on invested capital is extremely high, which validates both the technology spending and acquisitions. On the other hand, one could question whether all buybacks were done at sensible prices. We - as the valuation obsessed guys - are the devil’s advocate here, but we objectively admit our view is partially biased by the genius of hindsight, i.e. we started to evaluate company only after knowing about the 2026 drop.

Also, R&D and capex spending is still relatively small as a percent of revenue (6% combined in 2025), so some might worry about under-investment for long-term innovation, although so far the strategy is clearly paying off in profitability.

Guidance

Q3 2026 revenue is guided to $2.055-2.085B, implying 46-48% YoY growth. The $2.07B midpoint was roughly in line with, or slightly below, consensus near $2.08B. AppLovin gives no full-year revenue guidance, which is a pity, if you ask us. Street estimates are around $8.2B, or roughly 50% growth. Analysts will (or should :) watch whether advertising demand stays strong (no major signs of slowdown yet) and whether cost assumptions (e.g. SBC) align with guidance. We haven’t noticed major warning signs of cyclicality in Q2 commentary. Overall, in our view, the latest quarter reinforces that AppLovin’s fundamentals (growth, margins, cash flow) are powering ahead in line with past trends.

Valuation Overview

At the August 20, 2026 close of $308.77, AppLovin had roughly 335M shares outstanding, implying a market cap of about $103.5B. Using the latest Q2 balance sheet, with $3.05B of cash and $3.52B of debt, net debt is only about $0.46B and enterprise value roughly $104B.

The valuation has compressed dramatically. On a trailing basis, AppLovin has generated roughly $6.83B of revenue, $4.41B of continuing net income, $5.73B of adjusted EBITDA and about $4.51B of FCF. That puts the stock at roughly 23.5x earnings, 23x FCF and 18x adjusted EBITDA, with an FCF yield around 4.4%.

Forward valuation looks cheaper still. Consensus currently expects roughly $8.2B of 2026 revenue and about $15.9 of EPS, implying around 19x forward earnings and 13x EV/Sales. Those multiples are no longer obviously expensive given current growth and margins, but they depend heavily on earnings durability. If growth decelerates much faster than expected, today’s apparent cheapness could prove deceptive.

Key Uncertainties

The key question is no longer simply valuation, but whether the earnings supporting it are sustainable. Q3 guidance already implies growth slowing to 46-48%, while Axon model improvements can be uneven quarter to quarter. Competition, weaker ad demand, slower consumer adoption, regulation or rising AI infrastructure costs could all pressure growth. However, the underlying business still shows exceptional margins, cash generation and balance-sheet strength.

5 Strongest Qualities

  1. extraordinary revenue growth

  2. exceptionally high margins

  3. massive cash generation

  4. minimal debt

  5. exceptional capital efficiency

5 Main Concerns

  1. unpredictable Axon model improvements

  2. progressive growth deceleration

  3. unproven consumer advertising expansion

  4. intense competition from larger platforms

  5. regulatory and ad-cycle risks

Key KPIs to monitor

  1. Advertising revenue growth and guidance

  2. Net revenue per installation when disclosed

  3. Consumer advertiser spend and adoption

  4. Adjusted EBITDA margin

  5. FCF conversion and diluted share count

Our most important fundamental question:

Can AppLovin sustain its extraordinary growth and operating leverage as a now “pure” advertising platform, or will market and competitive pressures drive a much sharper growth slowdown?

Management Quality & Insider Activity

AppLovin remains heavily founder-led. Co-founder Adam Foroughi has served as CEO since 2011 and has overseen an unusually successful transformation, spanning from a mobile-app developer and advertising platform into a focused, AI-driven ad-tech business. The most important strategic decision was arguably recognising that AppLovin’s software was more valuable than the games it owned. Executing such transition successfully and possessing an ability to recognise a need for it in the first place speak volumes on its own.

As mentioned previously, management ultimately sold the Apps business in 2025 for approximately $716M of cash and equity consideration, allowing resources to concentrate on Axon. During the same year, AppLovin reported $4.0B of FCF, including discontinued Apps cash flows, and repurchased $2.2B of shares. That combination of strategic focus, product execution and increasingly aggressive buybacks reflects favourably on management’s capital allocation.

Foroughi is also unusually important to the investment case. Axon’s development, AppLovin’s entrepreneurial culture and its willingness to move rapidly into new advertising categories all remain closely tied to him. This creates genuine key-person risk. AppLovin has nevertheless taken steps to strengthen oversight. In April 2026, Foroughi relinquished the chairman role to independent director Craig Billings, while internal successors Giovanni Ge and Corina Cacovean were promoted to CTO and Chief Legal Officer respectively as long-serving executives transitioned out. The fact that both successors came from within suggests reasonable organisational depth rather than dependence on one small founding group that has a desire to manage everything.

Governance remains more complicated, though. AppLovin has a dual-class share structure in which Class B shares carry 20 votes each. Foroughi controlled approximately 61.6% of total voting power as of March 2026, while the voting agreement with Herald Chen and affiliated parties collectively covered 66.9%. Investors as ordinary shareholders thus have limited ability to influence board elections, transactions or any other major corporate decisions really... Founder control can support long-term decision-making, but it also weakens the normal checks available to outside investors.

Executive compensation is substantial but predominantly equity-based. Foroughi received approximately $13.0M in 2025 compensation, of which $12.6M consisted of stock awards. AppLovin pays no annual cash bonuses to executives and requires the CEO to maintain company equity worth at least 6x base salary. Foroughi comfortably exceeds that threshold.

The place where we need to stop, though, is insider activity. Foroughi sold roughly 183,000 directly owned shares across March and June 2026, worth approximately $87M, with additional shares sold by a children’s trust. Did we hear “taxes”? … Other insiders also sold substantial amounts, including Eduardo Vivas selling roughly 164,000 shares for $82.6M under a 10b5-1 plan, while retiring legal chief Victoria Valenzuela sold 20,000 shares for $11.3M. Director Maynard Webb sold another 3,076 shares in July under a pre-arranged 10b5-1 plan.

We wouldn’t treat those sales as proof that insiders expect deterioration. However, the actions certainly doesn’t spark confidence, either. It’s true that Foroughi still retains enormous economic exposure, including roughly 28M super-voting Class B shares as of the latest proxy. But the absence of meaningful open-market insider buying is notable, particularly after the recent share-price collapse. One would certainly thought that if you confidently believe in the story and future of your own company, you’d be more prone to buy its shares once they halved in value.

Overall, we still must claim that management execution has been exceptional, while governance is, in our view, less exceptional. Founder ownership provides strong alignment, but concentrated voting control and persistent insider selling deserve continued scrutiny. It would be a shame seeing this company turn to , i.e. a vehicle for value extraction from shareholders and transfer to founders.

Risk Factors

Company-Specific Operating Risks

Platform Concentration

Or, in other words, dependence on the mobile app ecosystem. AppLovin’s revenue remains heavily concentrated in mobile-app advertising, especially gaming, despite its emerging consumer and CTV businesses. A large share of revenue flows through a handful of distribution platforms (Apple’s App Store, Google Play, Meta’s mobile apps). This naturally creates platform concentration risk.

For example, any policy change by Apple or Google that restricts third-party ad tracking or prioritises their own networks could slam AppLovin’s growth. Indeed, Apple’s IDFA privacy change already forced AppLovin to adjust its targeting methods. If Meta or Google similarly alter their data-sharing rules or if any major app publisher reduces SDK usage, AppLovin could lose significant ad inventory.

In practice, losing access to a platform’s inventory (or falling out of favour with a partner) would immediately shrink revenue and reduce margin (since the fixed costs of the platform don’t fall). Public warning signs would instead include slowing revenue growth, weaker installation trends or deteriorating net revenue per installation when disclosed. AppLovin must continually invest in its relationships with these platforms and failure to do so would be directly visible in slowing growth or rising customer churn.

It’s also rather uncomfortable in the long term if your business model is heavily dependend on giant companies that are simultaneously your very competition (Meta, Google).

Customer & Vertical Concentration

Although no single client accounted for over 10% of revenue in 2023-2025, AppLovin’s customers aren’t evenly diversified across industries. Historically, its client base has been dominated by mobile game developers (including its former Apps business).

The recent effort to “expand our customer base” into e-commerce and other apps is still nascent. This concentration means that sector-specific slowdowns (e.g. a crash in casual gaming popularity or a saturation of gaming ads) would hit revenue disproportionately. Additionally, AppLovin’s customers are predominantly short-term advertisers (no long-term contracts), so even a small shift in marketing budgets can quickly hit topline. Because advertiser counts and top-10 spend are undisclosed, one should watch consumer-spend commentary, revenue growth and customer-concentration disclosures instead. If these plateau or shrink, it suggests AppLovin’s core market is peaking.

Dependence on Axon AI & Product Execution

AppLovin’s growth thesis hinges on its Axon machine-learning engine and MAX bidding platform delivering superior ROI. Any failure of these systems (whether due to technical bugs, algorithmic lag, or inability to adapt to new ad formats) would directly impair performance.

For example, if Axon’s optimisations yield lower conversion than expected (say due to biased training data or black-box opacity), clients could see underwhelming results and reallocate budgets. Because advertiser spending depends heavily on performance, sustained deterioration would likely cause budgets to move elsewhere and pressure revenue quickly. If competitors’ algorithms (Google’s or Meta’s AI) outpace Axon, AppLovin risks becoming the inferior solution. Public warning signs include weaker revenue per installation, installation volumes, guidance and management commentary on model performance.

Expansion Execution Risk

This is aboutthe new vertical push. AppLovin has begun targeting non-gaming advertisers (e-commerce, social apps) and new channels (CTV via Wurl). These markets have formidable incumbents with e-commerce advertisers already spending heavily on Google/Amazon ads, and CTV is dominated by companies like Roku, Comcast, etc.

Expanding into these areas requires significant execution risk. Missteps (such as misjudging customer needs, overspending on marketing, or delays in technology rollout) could lead to high costs without matching revenue. For instance, if e-commerce brands find AppLovin’s “black-box” AI too opaque (one buyer told AdExchanger that AppLovin’s platform offers only limited transparency), AppLovin might have trouble signing up large retailers. On the revenue statement, failed expansion would show up as rising SG&A/R&D with little revenue growth. If the contribution of these new segments persistently underperform relative to plans, it signals wasted investment.

Talent & Leadership Risk

As we mentioned above, the founder and CEO Adam Foroughi remains central to AppLovin’s strategy and Axon development. The company itself acknowledges its dependence on Foroughi, senior management and specialised engineering talent.

Losing key AI or data-science employees thus could slow product development, while competition for these workers could increase compensation and dilution. This is important particularly because AppLovin runs a relatively lean organisation.

Financial & Accounting Risks

Fixed Cloud-Computing Costs

AppLovin committed to spend at least $1.3B on cloud services over 3 years beginning in 2024. By June 2026, however, it had already paid $953.5M, leaving only about $347M. The commitment therefore remains a contractual minimum spend, but is materially less threatening than it appeared previously.

The larger long-term issue is that increasingly complex Axon models require continued compute spending. If revenue growth slows while infrastructure costs keep rising, margins would come under pressure.

Debt & Financial Commitments

AppLovin carries substantial gross debt, with approximately $3.5B of long-term debt at June 2026. However, this risk shouldn’t be overstated as the company also held $3.05B of cash and generated enormous cash flow, leaving net leverage at only around 0.1x trailing adjusted EBITDA. Most debt is fixed-rate and long-dated. Debt becomes a meaningful problem primarily if Axon’s earnings power deteriorates sharply or management adds leverage to fund buybacks or acquisitions.

Non-GAAP Accounting & Exclusions

AppLovin highlights adjusted EBITDA, which excludes costs such as stock-based compensation and certain non-recurring items. Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $1.61B, versus $1.49B of GAAP operating income, while SBC was approximately $86M. These adjustments acen’t currently hiding a weak underlying business, but investors should still focus on GAAP earnings and FCF rather than adjusted margins alone. Large future impairments or a widening gap between GAAP and adjusted results would require attention.

SBC Dilution

Equity awards dilute shareholders and count as operating expense. In 2025 AppLovin recognised $208M in equity comp, down from $357M in 2024, largely due to headcount changes. However, the company is also running a large buyback program to neutralise this dilution. If business falters, the company might scale back buybacks, leaving equity comp unneutralised and share count rising. The buyback pace is important to follow, as any sudden halt or major issuance (secondary offering, although none is announced) would dilute.

Tax Incentive Risk

AppLovin’s low tax rate benefits materially from Singapore tax incentives. These reduced its 2025 tax provision by $272M, or $0.80 per diluted share, and are expected to expire in June 2028 unless renewed. Failure to renew them, or adverse international tax changes, could raise AppLovin’s effective tax rate and reduce future EPS.

Competitive, Regulatory & Macroeconomic Risks

Intense Competition from Tech Giants

AppLovin operates in a cutthroat ad-tech market. Google (with its Ads and AdMob ecosystem) and Meta (Facebook/IG ads) control massive online ad budgets, and Unity (after merging with ironSource) remains a major competitor in mobile-game monetisation.

These competitors possess vast user data and can bundle advertising with popular developer tools. For example, Unity now offers LevelPlay (mediation) embedded in its engine, directly competing with AppLovin’s MAX mediation. AppLovin acknowledges the risk that competitors with entrenched positions could “bundle” their services, and that incumbent platforms like Apple or Google could leverage their own ad offerings.

In practice, Google could incentivise game developers to use AdMob instead of AppLovin, or Apple could further expand its App Store advertising business, further crowding the space. Such moves would siphon market share and compress AppLovin’s growth. An early warning is if AppLovin’s growth rate starts lagging behind industry ad spend growth. For instance, if consumer app ad spend rises but AppLovin’s revenue share falls, that signals displacement.

Securities Litigation & Residual Regulatory Risk

The SEC overhang has materially decreased. AppLovin disclosed in August 2026 that the SEC had concluded its inquiry with no recommended action. However, securities class-action and shareholder derivative litigation remain ongoing. The SEC outcome substantially reduces regulatory risk, but doesn’t really resolve the private claims or eliminate the reputational consequences of earlier allegations.

Macroeconomic & Geopolitical Uncertainty

Advertising is cyclical. During recessions or periods of weaker consumer spending, advertisers typically reduce budgets, which could slow AppLovin’s growth quickly. Expansion into e-commerce and other consumer categories may increase this sensitivity. International operations also expose the company to geopolitical disruption, changing trade policies and currency movements.

Technology & Cybersecurity Risks

Cybersecurity Breaches & Data Protection

AppLovin processes large volumes of advertiser, publisher and user data. A significant breach or prolonged outage could create regulatory liabilities, damage trust and disrupt campaigns. AppLovin says it hasn’t identified any cybersecurity incident that has materially affected the company to date, and it maintains formal security controls and board oversight, but the risk cannot be eliminated and needs to be considered at all times.

Technological Change & Obsolescence

This is one of the more important overall risks. AppLovin’s advantage depends heavily on Axon continuing to improve. Q2 2026 demonstrated the sensitivity when fewer meaningful model improvements contributed to slower-than-expected growth. AI also benefits competitors, meaning AppLovin cannot assume its technological lead is permanent. If Meta, Google or another platform achieves comparable advertising returns, budgets can move quickly, with AppLovin receiving a lot less of the Lovin.

Third-Party Service Dependencies

AppLovin relies on third-party cloud infrastructure, app stores and other technology providers to operate its platform. Outages, higher costs or changes in third-party policies could disrupt ad delivery or reduce Axon’s effectiveness. The greatest dependency is arguably not ordinary cloud hosting but the broader Apple and Google mobile ecosystems, which AppLovin doesn’t control.

Our Scenarios (3-5 Year Horizon): Bull, Base, Bear Case

We use a 3-to-5-year horizon to assess how AppLovin’s advertising growth, consumer expansion, Axon performance and margins could develop by 2029 and 2031. Note that these aren’t estimates of intrinsic value today. Instead, they represent potential future share prices if each operating scenario materialises, using normalised horizon-year earnings and scenario-appropriate valuation multiples. Our reference price is the August 20, 2026 close of $308.77.

Bull Case (20% Probability)

Key Assumptions

Axon maintains a substantial performance advantage, gaming remains healthy and AppLovin successfully establishes consumer advertising as a major second growth engine. Revenue continues compounding well above market growth, margins remain exceptional despite tax normalisation and higher infrastructure spending, and strong FCF supports continued share repurchases.

Financial Outcomes

Revenue reaches approximately $16.5B in 2029 and $23B in 2031, producing normalised EPS of roughly $32 and $47. Applying earnings multiples of 28x and 26x produces estimated share prices of approximately $900 in 3 years and $1,220 in 5 years.

From the $308.77 reference price, that represents annualised returns of approximately 43% over 3 years and 32% over 5 years.

Base Case (60% Probability)

Key Assumptions

Growth decelerates substantially from today’s 50%+ rates but remains strong as Axon continues improving and consumer advertising becomes a meaningful business without replicating gaming’s dominance. Normalised margins remain exceptionally high, while strong cash generation supports gradual share-count reduction.

Financial Outcomes

Revenue reaches approximately $14B in 2029 and $18B in 2031, producing normalised EPS of roughly $25 and $35. Applying earnings multiples of 25x and 23x produces estimated share prices of approximately $625 in 3 years and $800 in 5 years.

From the $308.77 reference price, that represents annualised returns of approximately 26% over 3 years and 21% over 5 years.

Bear Case (20% Probability)

Key Assumptions

Axon improvements slow materially, consumer advertising fails to become a major growth engine and competition increasingly pressures advertiser returns. Revenue growth falls toward high-single digits, while higher taxes, infrastructure spending and competitive investment push margins materially below current levels. Buybacks also become less aggressive.

Financial Outcomes

Revenue reaches approximately $10.5B in 2029 and $12B in 2031, producing normalised EPS of roughly $14 and $16. Applying earnings multiples of 16x produces estimated share prices of approximately $225 in 3 years and $250 in 5 years.

From the $308.77 reference price, that represents annualised returns of approximately -10% over 3 years and -4% over 5 years.

Moat Resilience Index™ (MRI)

Moat Strength: 6.5/10

AppLovin’s moat rests on Axon’s advertising performance, proprietary data generated across enormous transaction volumes, MAX distribution and deep positioning within mobile-app monetisation. The combination creates a powerful flywheel where better targeting improves advertiser returns, attracting more spend and generating additional data.

The score stops at 6.5 because switching costs are low, advertisers routinely use competing platforms and AppLovin must continuously outperform rather than rely on contractual lock-in. Its moat is proven in gaming, but whether that advantage transfers broadly into consumer advertising remains uncertain.

Moat Hate: 9/10

AppLovin has suffered an extraordinary valuation reset despite revenue still growing above 50%, adjusted EBITDA margins above 80% and massive free cash generation. The stock has fallen more than 50% in 2026 as investors increasingly question Axon durability, consumer expansion and future growth.

Sentiment is exceptionally weak. Minor disappointments have triggered double-digit declines, while major positives such as the SEC inquiry ending without recommended action produced little relief. The market has moved from pricing near-perfect execution to questioning whether AppLovin’s exceptional performance is sustainable at all. AppLovin is currently truly a Hated Moat.

Moat Vulnerability: 7/10

We believe AppLovin’s moat is powerful but unusually dependent on continued execution. Advertisers can move budgets quickly if Axon stops producing superior returns, while Meta, Google, Unity and other competitors possess enormous datasets, engineering resources and established advertiser relationships.

The largest vulnerabilities are technological stagnation, dependence on Apple and Google’s mobile ecosystems and failure to establish a meaningful moat outside gaming. If Axon retains its performance edge, these risks remain manageable. If that edge narrows, AppLovin has relatively little customer lock-in to protect its economics. In simplified and exaggerated manner, it could be said that if Google and Apple really wanted, they could virtually evaporate huge part of AppLovin’s moat within months, if not weeks.

Hated Moats Outperformance Score™ (HMOS): 65%

AppLovin receives an HMOS of 65/100, indicating a favourable but far from certain 5-year outperformance set-up.

The opportunity rests on exceptional cash generation, strong advertising growth, Axon maintaining its performance edge, successful expansion beyond gaming and a valuation that has reset sharply. The principal risks are faster growth deceleration, weaker model improvements, limited customer lock-in, failure in consumer advertising, platform dependence, tax normalisation, governance concerns and competition from much larger advertising ecosystems.

Conclusion

AppLovin sits in an unusual position where an exceptional business has become a difficult stock. Revenue is still growing above 50%, margins and cash generation remain extraordinary and the balance sheet is close to net cash. Yet the market has moved from rewarding exceptional execution to questioning whether that execution can be repeated at all.

The long-term case rests on Axon maintaining superior advertiser returns and transferring that advantage beyond gaming. AppLovin doesn’t need 50% growth forever, which would be unrealistic given market saturation and the law of large numbers. It does need growth to normalise gradually rather than collapse, though, while preserving enough of its extraordinary margins and cash generation. Even if that’s completely natural and even expected, combined with the current sentiment, normalisation / deceleration of growth is potentially a big problem for the currently already broken stock.

Also, the near-term problem is expectations. A strong quarter can now be dismissed as already expected, while even a small disappointment can be interpreted as evidence that Axon’s advantage is weakening. Q2 demonstrated how objectively excellent results can still produce severe stock declines when they fall short of near-perfect expectations.

This creates the risk of a negative expectations flywheel. Slower growth leads to lower estimates, lower estimates reinforce weaker sentiment and every disappointment further reduces confidence in the durability of the moat. AppLovin could therefore remain fundamentally strong while the stock stagnates or falls for considerably longer than investors expect. Our main thought here could be summarised as:

There are many ways for APP to disappoint the expectations embedded in its growth narrative, while relatively few ways to restore the market’s previous level of confidence.

However, sentiment cannot completely overpower growing cash flow per share indefinitely. If AppLovin continues compounding earnings, generates billions in FCF and repurchases shares, either the stock eventually responds or its valuation becomes increasingly difficult to reconcile with the underlying economics. Short-term sentiment never beats strong fundamentals and repeatedly good results in the long-term. The problem is, “short-term sentiment” can last much longer than expected, and long enough for the opportunity cost to start matter.

At $308.77, our base scenario reaches roughly $625 in 2029 and $800 in 2031, while the bear case remains around $225 and $250. The upside therefore appears attractive, but the path toward realising it could be volatile, nonlinear and dependent on rebuilding confidence in Axon’s durability.

Management deserves substantial credit for AppLovin’s transformation and extraordinary execution. Governance deserves more caution given concentrated founder control, persistent insider selling and limited open-market buying after the decline.

We believe that investors should focus primarily on advertising growth, Axon model performance, consumer adoption, net revenue per installation when disclosed, margins, FCF conversion and actual share-count reduction.

Final Verdict: MODERATE BUY

AppLovin qualifies as a Moderate Buy. The valuation reset, exceptional profitability, strong cash generation and still-rapid growth create favourable long-term asymmetry, but the stock currently faces a difficult expectations regime that prevents us from assigning higher conviction.

Our concern is not simply that growth will slow since it inevitably will. The greater risk is that expectations decline faster than fundamentals, creating an extended period where excellent operating performance continues to disappoint the market. Axon improvements are unpredictable, customer lock-in is limited and consumer advertising remains promising rather than proven.

There is also a genuine earnings-estimate risk. AppLovin can appear inexpensive on forward earnings while the stock continues declining if those earnings estimates are repeatedly revised downward. At today’s valuation, however, considerably less perfection is embedded than near the 2025 highs (logically :).

Based on the mentioned, we see AppLovin as a great business with a currently difficult stock setup. The market may require several quarters of consistent execution before restoring confidence, and even exceptional results may not immediately translate into higher prices. Price-action-of-the-stock-wise, think Adobe for the past 4-5 quarters type of scenario.

Our verdict is thus MODERATE BUY. The long-term risk-reward appears favourable, but we believe that investors should be prepared for the possibility that AppLovin continues delivering exceptional fundamentals for some time before sentiment (and the stock price itself with it) meaningfully improve.

AppLovin doesn’t really need the market to fall in love with it again the same way as it did in previous years. It eventually needs the market to stop becoming more pessimistic. That can be a hard task for a couple of quarters ahead. It can also be a great opportunity to own a fundamentally exceptional business.
